title: Review: Energy transfer and productivity; Succession; Nitrogen and phosphorus cycles; Carbon cycle and climate change
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EC06#t3 term and clue written for the game; EC04c#t1 term and clue written for the game; EC05b#t4 term and clue written for the game; EC07#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EC04c#N.2, EC05a#N.5a, EC05b#N.5, EC06#N.6, EC05a#N.9, EC05b#N.15, EC06#N.15, EC05a#N.12, EC05b#N.3, EC06#N.9, EC06#N.3. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Denitrification
items.clue: Bacteria convert NO₃⁻ back to N₂ in anaerobic, waterlogged soil

items.label: Trophic level
items.clue: Each one passes on only a small share of its energy, often around 10%

items.label: Combustion
items.clue: Burning of fossil fuels: the cause of the long-term rise in atmospheric CO₂

items.label: Pioneer species
items.clue: The first colonisers of bare ground, e.g. lichens, which need almost no soil

questions.stem: Food chains in most ecosystems have no more than four or five trophic levels. What is the reason for this restriction?

options.text: The number of trophic levels is set by the number of species in the community, and few communities have more than five.
The tissues of organisms higher in the chain contain less energy per gram, so a predator cannot gain enough energy from each meal.
Decomposers occupy the last trophic level of every chain and take the remaining energy, so no further consumers can be added.
So much energy is lost at each transfer that after a few levels too little remains to support a viable consumer population.

questions.explanation: Most energy at each level is lost as heat or passes to decomposers, so eventually there is not enough to sustain another level.

questions.stem: In an experiment, all the decomposers in a woodland soil are killed, but the trees keep growing for a while. Which change would follow over the next few years?

options.text: Dead leaves would pile up and the soil would run short of ions such as phosphate, so growth would slow.
Nothing would change, because elements are released from dead leaves automatically as they fall.
Only carbon recycling would stop; nitrogen and phosphorus would return to the soil as before.
The trees would lose their energy supply, because decomposers return energy from dead leaves to plants.

questions.stem: Which is an anthropogenic cause of the rise in the atmospheric concentration of methane since pre-industrial times?

options.text: Enteric fermentation in the growing numbers of ruminant farm livestock
Exhalation of waste gases by the greatly increased human population
Complete combustion of coal and petroleum in vehicles and power stations
Escape of ancient methane trapped in bubbles in melting polar ice

questions.explanation: Methanogenic archaea in the guts of cattle and other ruminants release methane, and livestock numbers have risen greatly.

questions.stem: A field is flooded for several weeks and the soil becomes waterlogged. Afterwards, the nitrate content of the soil is much lower. Which process best explains the loss?

options.text: Nitrification, which runs faster when water fills the air spaces in the soil
Nitrogen fixation, which converts the nitrate in the soil back into nitrogen gas
Denitrification by bacteria in the anaerobic soil, giving nitrogen gas
Ammonification, in which decomposers convert the nitrate into ammonium ions

questions.explanation: Waterlogged soil is anaerobic. Denitrifying bacteria use nitrate and release N₂, which escapes to the air.

questions.stem: Which statement about the combustion of biomass, peat, coal, oil and natural gas is correct?

options.text: All formed from organisms at about the same time in the distant past, so burning any of them has the same significance for the carbon cycle.
Burning biomass such as wood releases no carbon dioxide because it is renewable, whereas burning the fossil fuels does release it.
All release carbon dioxide that was originally fixed by photosynthesis, at dates ranging from recent years to hundreds of millions of years ago.
Coal, oil and natural gas release carbon of mineral origin that did not come from living organisms, unlike biomass and peat.

questions.explanation: Biomass may be a few years old, peat thousands of years, coal, oil and gas millions; all began as carbon fixed by autotrophs.

questions.stem: At a monitoring station in Tasmania, in the Southern Hemisphere, carbon dioxide shows a much smaller yearly swing than at Mauna Loa, but a similar long-term rise. Which explanation fits both observations?

options.text: The swing is small because fewer people burn fuel for winter heating there; the rise is because more people breathe out CO₂.
The swing is small because the south has much less land and plant life; the rise is from combustion CO₂ mixing worldwide.
The swing is small because southern plants stop respiring in winter; the rise is because volcanoes have become more active.
Both are measurement errors, because living things are far too small to change the carbon dioxide in the whole atmosphere.

questions.stem: A farmer grows clover, a legume, in a field for a year, then ploughs the clover into the soil. Wheat sown next needs much less nitrogen fertiliser than wheat sown after wheat. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Clover roots absorb nitrogen gas from the air in the soil, and the wheat roots then take up this same nitrogen gas.
Bacteria in the clover's root nodules fixed nitrogen gas; decomposers later released it into the soil.
The clover made new nitrogen atoms from the sugars it produced in photosynthesis, so the soil now holds more nitrogen.
The clover's own root cells fixed nitrogen gas, so no bacteria or other microorganisms were needed to enrich the soil.

questions.stem: A peat bog has stored carbon for thousands of years in waterlogged soil. It is drained for farmland, and the peat dries out. What happens to much of the carbon in the peat?

options.text: Air reaches the peat, so decomposers break it down and respire it, releasing its carbon as CO₂.
It stays locked in the soil, because decomposition moves carbon into the soil rather than out of it.
Drying slows the decay, as wet conditions speed up rotting, so the soil stores even more carbon.
The crops' roots absorb it from the soil and build it into their biomass.

questions.explanation: Waterlogging kept O₂ out and decay slow. Drained, the peat is decomposed and the bog turns from a store into a source of CO₂.

questions.stem: At Mauna Loa, atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration rises to a peak each May and falls to a minimum each September or October, a swing of several parts per million. What causes this annual fluctuation?

options.text: People burn more fuel for heating in the Northern Hemisphere winter, so combustion raises carbon dioxide until spring and it falls again in summer.
Plants respire only in winter, when they cannot photosynthesise, so carbon dioxide is released only in the cold months and absorbed in the warm months.
In the Northern Hemisphere growing season photosynthesis exceeds respiration, drawing carbon dioxide down; in autumn and winter respiration exceeds photosynthesis.
Biological processes are too small to change the whole atmosphere, so the regular swing must be an artefact of the measuring instruments at the observatory.

questions.stem: What are the benefits to each partner in the relationship between a legume and the bacteria in its root nodules?

options.text: The bacteria supply the plant with nitrogen gas from the soil; the plant supplies the bacteria with oxygen.
The bacteria supply the plant with fixed nitrogen as ammonia or amino acids; the plant supplies the bacteria with sugars.
The plant gains fixed nitrogen from the bacteria; the bacteria gain nothing from the plant but are not harmed by living in the nodule.
The bacteria take sugars from the roots and give the plant nothing, so the nodules are a mild infection the plant tolerates.

questions.explanation: Rhizobium in the nodules converts N₂ into ammonia, which the plant uses to make amino acids. The plant supplies sugars from photosynthesis and a protected home: both benefit.

questions.stem: Which statement about the recycling of chemical elements in ecosystems is correct?

options.text: Only carbon is recycled; the other elements are absorbed from the soil, used by organisms and then used up, so they must be replaced.
Elements are released from dead organisms automatically as they die, so decomposers play only a minor part in recycling them.
Both the chemical elements and the energy in dead organisms are recycled by decomposers and returned to producers for reuse.
All elements required by organisms are recycled; decomposers release them from dead matter in forms that autotrophs can take up.

questions.explanation: All elements used by organisms are recycled. Decomposers break down the carbon compounds of dead matter and return the elements as simple inorganic substances.
